_readme: Axis pairs the field treats as a tradeoff. Read by FD 4 scoring, spec 5.1.1:
an item that improves one axis WITHOUT the loss along its pair has collapsed
the tradeoff, and that is the only route to a 4.
Applied by scripts/backfill-axis-pairs.js (dry-run by default). Requires
migration 012.
axis_a and axis_b must match the `axis` wording on frontier_records for the
same subfield, or the pair cannot be evaluated against anything. The loader
checks this and warns; it does not silently accept a dangling pair.
why_binding is the text a score of 4 has to cite. It records why the FIELD
has treated the two as coupled. It is NOT a claim that the tradeoff is real
or permanent: an item that collapses it is precisely the item proving the
belief wrong, which is why that item scores 4.
strength is how firmly the coupling is held.
settled    the field designs around it as a given
contested  actively disputed, or already partly broken
asserted   stated in our own spec or by one group, not independently
established. Default, and deliberately the humblest option.
SEEDED FROM THE PAIRS THE SPEC NAMES, restricted to those where BOTH axes
already exist as records. Section 5.1.1 lists four families: channel count
against chronic viability, invasiveness against bandwidth, selectivity
against coverage, and efficacy against titration burden. The first two are
instantiated below. The other two are NOT, because no record in this database
measures selectivity, coverage, or titration burden yet. They are listed in
_not_yet_instantiable as a work queue rather than invented here.
Every entry below names two axes that are genuinely stored, so each one can
actually be evaluated. Adding a pair whose axes do not exist buys nothing.

_comment: Spec 5.1.1 names these two families and this database has no axis for
either side. Skipped by the loader. Create the records first, then move
selectivity against coverage       needs a stimulation-selectivity axis
efficacy against titration burden  needs a programming/titration burden

intracortical-channels-vs-chronic-life.axis_b: chronic implantation duration, intracortical Utah array, human tetraplegia/paralysis clinical trial
intracortical-channels-vs-chronic-life.why_binding: Raising channel count means more penetrating shanks and more surface area exposed to tissue, which the field has treated as necessarily shortening chronic viability. Named in spec 5.1.1 as the canonical example of a binding tradeoff.
intracortical-channels-vs-chronic-life.notes: Sourced from section 5.1.1 of docs/neurobase-potential-impact-build-spec-v1.0.md, which names channel count against chronic viability. Not independently sourced to a study.

ecog-electrode-count-vs-chronic-use.axis_a: ECoG grid electrode count for word/gesture decoding
ecog-electrode-count-vs-chronic-use.axis_b: Chronic BCI/nightmode use duration, long-term deployment
ecog-electrode-count-vs-chronic-use.why_binding: The same channel-count against chronic-viability coupling as intracortical arrays, applied to surface grids: denser grids mean more interconnect and more encapsulation surface, which has been treated as shortening usable deployment.
ecog-electrode-count-vs-chronic-use.notes: Same family as intracortical-channels-vs-chronic-life. Sourced from spec 5.1.1, not from a study.

ecog-electrode-count-vs-power.axis_a: ECoG grid electrode count for word/gesture decoding
ecog-electrode-count-vs-power.axis_b: Power consumption, neural signal processing hardware (ASIC/FPGA)
ecog-electrode-count-vs-power.why_binding: Each additional recording channel adds an amplifier and digitisation path, so channel count and power draw have been treated as scaling together. Power is the constraint on a fully implanted device, so this coupling bounds how large an implanted array can be.
ecog-electrode-count-vs-power.notes: An instance of scale against a resource cost. Not named directly in the spec; recorded as asserted because it is an engineering coupling this database has not independently sourced.

materials-thickness-vs-chronic-life.why_binding: Thinner probes reduce tissue displacement and the foreign-body response, but thinner encapsulation has been treated as necessarily failing sooner, since the barrier against fluid ingress is what sets device lifetime.
materials-thickness-vs-chronic-life.notes: The invasiveness against durability form of the invasiveness family in spec 5.1.1. Not independently sourced to a study.

materials-thickness-vs-impedance.axis_b: electrode impedance, neural interface, in vitro/in vivo
materials-thickness-vs-impedance.why_binding: Smaller and thinner electrode sites present less surface area, and lower surface area raises impedance and therefore noise. The field has treated shrinking a site as necessarily costing signal quality.
materials-thickness-vs-impedance.notes: The invasiveness against bandwidth family in spec 5.1.1, in its impedance form. Not independently sourced to a study.

minimally-invasive-diameter-vs-snr.axis_b: SNR improvement for evoked/spontaneous neural signals, minimally invasive electrode vs conventional
minimally-invasive-diameter-vs-snr.why_binding: A narrower electrode causes less insertion trauma but couples to fewer neurons and has a smaller recording surface, which the field has treated as necessarily costing signal-to-noise.
minimally-invasive-diameter-vs-snr.notes: The invasiveness against bandwidth family in spec 5.1.1. Not independently sourced to a study.
